recap-class10.script: Let's take sixty seconds to remember where we've been. A model is just a learned relationship — features go in, a target comes out, and training means fitting that relationship to data by walking downhill on our loss until it stops falling. We judge only on test data, and we never trust predictions far outside our training range. Here's the beautiful part: today we keep all of that machinery and change exactly one thing — the target becomes a category instead of a number. Not "how many metres away," but "is it a real object, yes or no?"

quiz-warmup.script: Picture your car's camera spotting a blob on the road — is it a real pedestrian or just a shadow? You might think, "I'll just feed the confidence score into the linear regression we built last class." But here's the trouble: a line can output any number at all, from way below zero to way above one. So it might spit out negative three or positive eight — and those aren't probabilities, and they aren't yes-or-no answers. Today we fix that by bolting one small function onto the end, the sigmoid, which squeezes any number neatly between zero and one.

story-perceptron.script: Back in 1958, a man named Frank Rosenblatt built something called the Perceptron, and the New York Times announced it would soon walk, talk, see, write, and even become conscious of its own existence. It did none of that. Underneath those wild headlines was a simple machine that draws a straight line between two groups of dots — almost exactly what you'll build today. And notice how that happened: a modest result met an eager press office and an excited reporter, and a myth was born that outlived the machine. When the hype collapsed, funding vanished — but the humble idea survived, and it's now inside almost everything.

concept-categories.script: Last class we asked "how much?" — predicting a number like a price or a distance. Today the question changes to "which one?" Is this email spam or not, is this tumour benign or malignant? Here's the piece I really want you to write down: logistic regression doesn't hand you a label. It gives you a probability between zero and one, and then you choose the cut-off that turns that into a decision. That extra step sounds like a small technicality, but it's actually the most powerful choice in the entire model — it's what lets the same trained model be cautious or aggressive depending on what you need.

concept-sigmoid.script: So here's the one new gadget we're adding. Take the straight line from last class, get its output — we'll call it z — and push it through this S-shaped function. Whatever goes in, whatever huge number, out comes something between zero and one, which we read as a probability. When z is zero you land right at fifty-fifty, pure uncertainty; big positive z pushes you toward confident one, big negative toward confident zero — but it never quite touches either end, so the model is never absolutely certain. And because of this curve, we swap our loss too: cross-entropy punishes confident wrong answers hard and keeps pushing where squared error would leave training crawling.

quiz-sigmoid.script: Here's a subtle one. Your model spits out 0.52 for a detection — what has it actually told you? It's basically saying "I'm barely more than a coin flip on this," yet because 0.52 clears the 0.5 threshold, it gets stamped REAL, same label a confident 0.99 would get. That's the danger: if you only keep the final label, you throw away how unsure the model really was. And in a self-driving car, a nervous 0.52 and a rock-solid 0.99 should absolutely not trigger the same response.

concept-decision-boundary.script: Here's the beautiful part: when you set the probability to one half, you're really just drawing a straight line through your data. Everything on one side gets called a real object, everything on the other side a false alarm — so that line literally is your model, just two weights and an intercept. Notice these three or four dots sitting on the wrong side; that's not a mistake, that's what messy real data looks like. And look how a point hugging the line and a point far away can share the same label but wildly different confidence — hold onto that, because it's exactly why we'll want to move the threshold.

concept-accuracy-lies.script: Here's a number that will lie to your face: 96% accurate. Imagine a model watching dashcam footage where only 8 out of 200 frames contain a pedestrian. If it just says "no pedestrian" every single time, never even looking, it's right 192 times — that's 96% accuracy — and yet it catches zero of the actual pedestrians. So instead of accuracy, we ask: of the real pedestrians, what fraction did we catch? That's recall, and here it's zero. Whenever one class is rare — disease, fraud, pedestrians — accuracy flatters you, so never report it alone.

case-av-classification.script: Let's ground this in something real: a self-driving car, dozens of times every second, asking one question — is that a real object, or just a false alarm? It looks at features like the detector's confidence and the height of the box around the object, and it has to decide, one or zero. Now here's the part that isn't maths: braking for a plastic bag is annoying, but not braking for a person is catastrophic. Those two mistakes are not equal, so where you set the threshold is a value judgement — no dataset on Earth will pick that number for you.

discuss-costly-errors.script: Here's a question I want you to really chew on: which mistake is worse, a wrong yes or a wrong no? Think about a spam filter — if it wrongly flags a job offer as spam, that opportunity vanishes forever, but a wrong "not spam" just costs you two seconds of annoyance. So pick a case, like cancer screening or airport security, and figure out who actually pays for each kind of error. Then wrestle with the hard part: should the model lean one way on purpose, and who gets to draw that line? Grab a partner for three minutes and post your best example and your best "who decides" answer.

Keep an eye on that weight, because it never quite stops growing, and Challenge 1 asks you why.

We train a model on two features—confidence and box height—and then we do the experiment that actually matters: we slide the decision threshold up and down and watch which mistakes we trade for which. And don't miss that accuracy trap at the bottom—a model that's ninety-six percent accurate while never spotting a pedestrian is worse than useless.

For your exit ticket, give me a real example where a wrong "yes" hurts more than a wrong "no." Next time we meet models that don't draw lines at all — they ask questions you can actually read.

backup-multiclass.script: So far we've been asking yes-or-no questions, but what happens when you've got pedestrians, cars, and cyclists all at once? One approach is to train a separate detector for each class and just trust whichever one is most confident. The other is softmax — a single model that spits out a score for every class, all adding up to one. And here's the exciting part: that softmax layer sits at the end of nearly every modern neural network, including the one that decides the next word in ChatGPT.

backup-precision-recall.script: Let's get these four boxes straight, because they matter. A false positive is a false alarm; a false negative is a miss — and those are completely different mistakes that should never be lumped together. Here's the trick to remember: precision asks, when I raise the alarm, how often am I right? Recall asks, of everything I should have caught, how much did I actually catch? And watch what happens with the threshold — drop it low and you catch everything but half your alarms are junk; push it high and every alarm is right but you miss real objects. There's no magic setting that wins both.
